prompt: A producer's sale is written by the leader, but the acknowledgement is lost. What does the producer know?

choices.text: That the sale was written, since the leader never fails silently
choices.why: It received nothing, so it cannot tell a lost reply from a lost write.

choices.text: Nothing: written and unacknowledged looks like never written
choices.why: Right. That is the first gap, and retrying it can write twice.

choices.text: That the sale was lost, because no reply came
choices.why: It may well be on disk; the reply is what was lost.

choices.text: Which offset it was written at
choices.why: The offset comes in the reply, which never arrived.

prompt: Match each order of steps to what a crash between them causes.

pairs.right: the interrupted messages are never processed
the interrupted messages are processed again
the message may be written twice

right_distractors: the message is corrupted on disk

prompt: Why can a consumer whose processing writes to another Kafka topic close its gap, while one that writes to PostgreSQL cannot do it the same way?

choices.text: PostgreSQL is slower than Kafka, so it cannot keep up with a transaction
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with whether two writes can share a transaction.

choices.text: Kafka keeps messages for longer
choices.why: Retention is not the point; atomicity is.

choices.text: Both steps are Kafka writes there, so one transaction holds both
choices.why: Right. The output and the offset commit can share a Kafka transaction; a database row cannot.

choices.text: PostgreSQL cannot be read by a consumer
choices.why: The question is about writing to it, not reading.

prompt: A consumer in at-most-once mode reads batches of ten from 50 sales and crashes after processing the 25th. On restart it processes the rest. How many sales are never processed?
hint: The third batch was committed before it was processed.

prompt: After the at-most-once crash, the file holds 45 different ids. How would anybody find out five sales are missing?

choices.text: The consumer prints an error for each
choices.why: It printed nothing about them: they were committed as handled.

choices.text: Kafka marks them as unread
choices.why: The committed offset says they were read.

choices.text: Only by counting against the topic
choices.why: Right. A loss is silent; the file is simply shorter.

choices.text: The file contains blank lines where they were
choices.why: Nothing is written for a sale that is never processed.

prompt: Which of these is the best fit for at most once?

choices.text: Payments to suppliers
choices.why: A lost payment is worse than a repeated one only if both are caught; neither is acceptable silently.

choices.text: A sample of page views feeding a rough dashboard
choices.why: Right. A few lost events change little, and a duplicate would distort it the same way.

choices.text: The stock count shown on the website
choices.why: Every lost sale makes the stock wrong for good.

choices.text: The nightly feed of every sale to the accountant, for the tax return
choices.why: Accounting needs every sale.

prompt: Same 50 sales, batches of ten, crash after processing the 25th, but in at-least-once mode. How many sales are processed twice?
hint: The last commit was after the second batch.

prompt: After that at-least-once crash and restart, how many lines does the output file hold for the 50 sales?
A consumer catches every exception from its processing, logs it and carries on, then commits the batch. What guarantee does it really have?

choices.text: At least once, since it commits after processing
choices.why: The failed message is covered by the commit and never retried.

choices.text: Exactly once
choices.why: Nothing makes the effect atomic with the commit.

choices.text: None for the failed messages: they vanish
choices.why: Right. It made them disappear on purpose; they belong in a dead-letter topic.

choices.text: At most once, but only during rebalances
choices.why: Rebalances have nothing to do with swallowed exceptions.

prompt: Why is at least once the usual choice, rather than at most once?

choices.text: It is faster
choices.why: Commit order changes outcomes, not speed in any meaningful way.

choices.text: A duplicate is visible to a reader that keeps ids; a loss leaves no trace
choices.why: Right. Choose the failure that can be repaired, and repair it downstream.

choices.text: Kafka refuses to run at most once
choices.why: The order of two calls in the consumer decides it; Kafka allows either.

choices.text: It never produces duplicates in practice
choices.why: The run in this lesson produced five.

prompt: A Python program uses confluent-kafka and sets nothing about idempotence. Is its producer idempotent?

choices.text: Yes, as in every client since Kafka 3.0
choices.why: That default is the Java client's; librdkafka keeps its own.

choices.text: No: librdkafka defaults to false
choices.why: Right. The dump shows producerId -1 for tills.py's batch.

choices.text: Yes, whenever acks=all
choices.why: acks=all is required by idempotence, not the same thing as it.

choices.text: Only on topics with one partition
choices.why: Partition count has nothing to do with the producer's setting.

prompt: In a log dump, a batch from a producer without idempotence shows `producerId: ___`.
An idempotent producer crashes after sending a sale and, on restart, sends the same sale again. What happens?

choices.text: The broker refuses it, because the sequence was already written
choices.why: The restarted program has a new PID, so its sequences start again.

choices.text: It is written twice
choices.why: Right. Idempotence protects retries inside one producer session, not resends after a restart.

choices.text: The producer refuses to start until the old PID expires
choices.why: An idempotent producer starts with a new PID at once.

choices.text: Kafka merges the two into one record
choices.why: Kafka never merges records by content.

prompt: Which settings come with enable.idempotence=true in librdkafka? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: acks=all
choices.why: Yes: a configuration with acks=1 is refused.

choices.text: At most five requests in flight per connection
choices.why: Yes: more is refused.

choices.text: Retries without limit inside message.timeout.ms
choices.why: Yes: retrying is safe once sequences are checked.

choices.text: isolation.level=read_committed
choices.why: That is a consumer setting, about transactions.

choices.text: A transactional.id
choices.why: Only transactions need one; idempotence works without it.

prompt: A transaction of five sales is aborted. What happens to the five records?

choices.text: They are never written to the log
choices.why: They are written at once; the dump showed them at offsets 6 to 10.

choices.text: They are deleted from the log by the abort
choices.why: A log is append-only; an abort adds a marker.

choices.text: They stay in the log, hidden from read_committed readers
choices.why: Right. A read_uncommitted reader still sees them.

choices.text: They are moved to a dead-letter topic for somebody to look at later
choices.why: Kafka moves nothing; dead-letter topics are written by programs.

prompt: Two transactions of five records each go to an empty single-partition topic, one committed and one aborted. What is the partition's end offset afterwards?
hint: Each transaction ends with a marker that takes an offset.

prompt: A Java consumer with default settings reads a topic written by eos_copy.py. What does it see?

choices.text: Only committed records, like every consumer
choices.why: Java's default is read_uncommitted.

choices.text: Nothing until it sets a transactional.id
choices.why: That is a producer setting.

choices.text: The aborted copies as well
choices.why: Right. It would count 22 where 20 were committed.

choices.text: An error, since transactional topics need special consumers
choices.why: Any consumer reads them; the isolation level decides what it sees.

prompt: A consumer that must not see aborted records sets `isolation.level` to ___.
In eos_copy.py, how does the consumer's position reach __consumer_offsets?

choices.text: Through auto commit, every five seconds
choices.why: Auto commit is off.

choices.text: Through `consumer.commit()` after each batch
choices.why: The program never calls commit.

choices.text: Inside the producer's transaction
choices.why: Right. Output and offsets commit together.

choices.text: It does not; the position is kept only in the consumer's memory until it closes
choices.why: The group's offset was 55 at the end.

prompt: eos_copy.py crashed after reading 25 sales in batches of ten. From which offset did the restart read?
Why does a read_committed count of big-sales match the source exactly, while a read_uncommitted count has two more?

choices.text: The aborted batch's two copies stay in the log, hidden only from committed readers
choices.why: Right. The abort marks them; it does not remove them.

choices.text: The restart copied two sales twice
choices.why: The restart's copies were committed once; the extras are the aborted ones.

choices.text: The idempotent producer added two records
choices.why: idempotent.py wrote to sales, and those were small sales.

choices.text: read_uncommitted counts the transaction markers
choices.why: Markers are never delivered to applications.

prompt: eos_copy.py also sends an email per big sale. After a crash and restart, what happens to the emails of the aborted batch?

choices.text: They are cancelled by the abort
choices.why: An email cannot be unsent; the abort only hides Kafka records.

choices.text: They are sent again
choices.why: Right. The effect is outside the transaction.

choices.text: They are held until the transaction commits
choices.why: Nothing holds an email; it went when send was called.

choices.text: Kafka sends them for the program
choices.why: Kafka has no part in sending email.

prompt: What does "exactly-once effect" mean outside Kafka, in the honest sense the lesson gives it?

choices.text: Every message is delivered exactly once
choices.why: Delivery stays at least once; the effect is what is made exact.

choices.text: A two-phase commit joins Kafka and the database
choices.why: Kafka does not offer one, for good reasons.

choices.text: Duplicates arrive, and the result is as if each came once
choices.why: Right. The receiving side tolerates repeats.

choices.text: Kafka's transactions extend to any database that supports them
choices.why: They cover Kafka writes only.

prompt: Put the steps of one eos_copy.py batch in order.
items: produce the big sales to big-sales

prompt: A team's consumer reads sales and inserts rows into PostgreSQL. They switch on enable.idempotence and transactions in their producer and expect no duplicate rows. What did they miss?

choices.text: Nothing: those two settings make the pipeline exactly once
choices.why: They cover Kafka writes; the database insert is outside.

choices.text: The repeat sits between the row and the offset commit, outside any Kafka transaction
choices.why: Right. That is lesson 8.

choices.text: They need more partitions
choices.why: Partitions do not change the gap between effect and commit.

choices.text: PostgreSQL must be switched to read_committed
choices.why: That is a Kafka consumer setting, and it does not reach the database.
